title: The shipwreck (Acts 27–28)
hook: two weeks of storm, Paul breaks bread on deck, 276 swim to Malta, and a viper bites harmlessly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul in Athens, quoting the poets on their own hill. Your line was in him we live. What good did you find on the other side? Day eighty-six.

Some weeks are all storm. One thing breaks, then another, and you stop being able to see the sky. Now board a cargo ship in the Mediterranean, late in the sailing season. On board is Paul, not as a passenger but as a prisoner, being taken to Rome for trial under a Roman officer named Julius. Paul warns them it's too late in the year to sail on. Nobody listens. Then a violent wind comes down off the island of Crete, the ship is caught, and they can't turn her into it. They lash ropes around the hull to hold it together. They throw the cargo overboard, then the ship's gear. For day after day there's no sun, no stars. And Luke, who writes this part as we, as if he's on board, says all hope that we should be saved was taken away.
screen: `A PRISONER ON A CARGO SHIP.` → `THE WIND OFF CRETE.` → `NO SUN, NO STARS.`

segments.voice: In the middle of it, Paul stands up among the exhausted crew and says, in the King James Bible: "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship." An angel stood by me last night, he says. And again: "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God." Be of good cheer is the King James wording for today's line. The Greek means something like be good-spirited. Take heart. On the fourteenth night they sense land is near. Some sailors try to slip away in the lifeboat, and are stopped. And just before dawn, with everyone starving and terrified, Paul does something completely ordinary. He tells them to eat. You've gone two weeks without a real meal, he says, and this is for your health. Then, Luke says, "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." Took, gave thanks, broke. Luke's words for the Last Supper, now on the deck of a storm-battered ship, among soldiers, sailors and prisoners. And they all take heart and eat. Luke even gives the head count: two hundred and seventy-six people. At daybreak the ship runs aground and breaks apart. Those who can swim jump first; the rest float in on planks. Every one of them reaches the shore. It's Malta, and the islanders build a fire in the cold rain. A viper comes out of the firewood and fastens onto Paul's hand. The locals decide he must be a murderer. He shakes it into the fire, and nothing happens. So they change their minds and decide he's a god.
screen: `BE OF GOOD CHEER.` · `THIS IS FOR YOUR HEALTH.` · `HE TOOK BREAD, AND GAVE THANKS.` · `276, ALL SAFE TO LAND.` · then, large: `TAKE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something steadying in a hard week. If you have something near you, a piece of bread, a cracker, fruit, a cup of tea, take it now. If not, just picture it. Before you eat, stop. Hold it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it, as Paul did on the deck. If you don't, just notice where it came from, and how many hands it passed through. Then eat it slowly, the way someone eats who hasn't eaten properly in a while. Let your body be steadied, one bite at a time. The bell holds the time.
The shipwreck. Fourteen days of storm, bread broken on a storm-battered deck, and two hundred and seventy-six people safe on Malta.
Your line: take heart. Today, in the storm of the week, eat one proper meal, sitting down, and let it steady you. Tomorrow, Paul's letters as real mail. Day eighty-six.

howItsDone: Many Christians give thanks before meals, as Paul does on the deck. In Malta, Paul's shipwreck is remembered every February 10 with a public holiday and feast, and Maltese tradition traces the island's faith to it.

fork.reveal: he urges them all to eat, takes bread, gives thanks in front of everyone, breaks it and begins to eat. then they all take heart.

original.note: Greek: be of good spirit, take heart. Paul says it twice on the ship (Acts 27:22, 25).

trapdoor: what you thought: an adventure story with a snake at the end.
what it means: in the worst of the storm, a prisoner tells everyone to take heart, and to eat, and breaks bread on the deck.
what a scholar hears: Luke writes it as we, as if on board, and describes the bread with the words of the Last Supper: took, gave thanks, broke.

notes: The 'we' passages: the script says Luke writes 'as if he's on board'; tradition names Luke as the companion, and scholars debate it. Confirm phrasing.
276 (Acts 27:37): some manuscripts read a different number (e.g., 76); KJV and most texts read 276.
Feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck in Malta, February 10, a public holiday; confirm.
The eucharistic echo (took, gave thanks, broke) is widely noted; churches differ on whether this meal was a Eucharist. Not claimed in the script.

Review (days 76–93 editor pass, 2026-10-01): 'the same words as ... the road to Emmaus' was inaccurate (Luke 24:30 has 'blessed', not 'gave thanks'), now only the Last Supper (Luke 22:19); the ship was not yet sinking when Paul broke bread (it breaks up at daybreak, 27:41), now 'storm-battered'; 'old English' now 'the King James wording'; cut 'the most ordinary thing' and the hook's 'Now picture'; howItsDone's 'many Maltese Christians' now 'Maltese tradition'.
